title: Burgenland
description: Austria's warm east: Blaufränkisch reds and the noble rot sweet wines of Lake Neusiedl.
L: Explain the role of Lake Neusiedl

Burgenland is Austria's easternmost state, a long strip along the Hungarian border, south-east of Vienna. It belonged to Hungary until 1921. It has about 11,700 hectares of vines. Key areas include Neusiedlersee, around the lake; Leithaberg, on the hills to the west; Mittelburgenland; and Eisenberg in the south.

Burgenland has a warm, dry Pannonian climate, influenced by the Hungarian plain: hot summers, cold winters and plenty of sun. It's Austria's warmest wine region, which is why it's the country's red wine heartland. Soils vary: limestone and schist on the Leithaberg, clay in Mittelburgenland, gravel and sand by the lake.
Why is Burgenland Austria's red wine heartland?
Its warm Pannonian climate ripens red grapes
Warmth from the Hungarian plain helps reds ripen.

Lake Neusiedl, Neusiedlersee, is a large, shallow steppe lake, about 320 km2 but only about 1 to 2 m deep, on the border with Hungary. It warms the area and, in autumn, creates mist and humidity that favour noble rot. The lake and its reed beds are a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a national park.
Not true. It's large but only about 1 to 2 m deep.

Its Pannonian climate makes it Austria's red heartland
Shallow Lake Neusiedl brings warmth and autumn mist

Blaufränkisch is the signature: dark cherry, blackberry, pepper and spice, with fresh acidity and firm tannin. Zweigelt, Austria's most planted red, a 1922 cross of Blaufränkisch and St. Laurent, gives soft, cherry reds. St. Laurent gives Pinot-like elegance. Pinot Noir, Merlot and Cabernet also appear in blends.

Welschriesling, unrelated to Riesling, is widely grown, especially for sweet wines. Chardonnay, locally Morillon in parts of Austria, Pinot Blanc, Grüner Veltliner and Furmint, revived near Rust, also grow here. Sweet wines often blend several white grapes affected by noble rot.
Match each grape to its role.
Burgenland grows reds and sweet whites.
Welschriesling has nothing to do with Riesling. Despite the name, they're not related.
Which grapes were crossed to create Zweigelt?
Zweigelt and St. Laurent complete the reds

Blaufränkisch, called Kékfrankos in Hungary and Lemberger in Germany, gives dark, spicy reds with black cherry, blackberry, black pepper and a mineral edge. Its acidity is high, its tannin firm but fine. It's often compared to Pinot Noir for transparency and to Syrah for spice. It ripens late and needs warm sites.

Mittelburgenland, called Blaufränkischland, around Deutschkreutz and Horitschon, has heavy clay, giving full, dark wines. Leithaberg, on limestone and schist, gives fresh, mineral, elegant wines. Eisenberg, in the south, on iron-rich schist, gives spicy, firm wines. Each has a DAC for Blaufränkisch.
What is Blaufränkisch called in Germany?
Lemberger in Württemberg; Kékfrankos in Hungary.

Austria's DAC system links regions to typical grapes. Mittelburgenland DAC, created in 2005, was Burgenland's first, for Blaufränkisch. Leithaberg DAC allows Blaufränkisch for reds and Pinot Blanc, Chardonnay, Grüner Veltliner and Neuburger for whites. Eisenberg DAC is Blaufränkisch. Reserve marks riper, longer-aged wines.
Wachau is for Grüner Veltliner and Riesling.
Blaufränkisch is spicy, dark and fresh
Mittelburgenland is full; Leithaberg mineral; Eisenberg spicy
DACs link each area to Blaufränkisch
Explain how the lake creates noble rot

Around Lake Neusiedl, autumn mists from the shallow water, followed by warm, sunny days, create ideal conditions for noble rot, Botrytis cinerea, almost every year. That makes the area one of the most reliable sources of sweet wine in the world. Illmitz and Apetlon, on the east shore, are famous for it.

Austria uses Prädikat categories similar to Germany's: Spätlese, Auslese, Beerenauslese, Eiswein, Strohwein or Schilfwein, from grapes dried on straw or reeds, and Trockenbeerenauslese. Ausbruch, between BA and TBA, is a historic style. Grapes include Welschriesling, Chardonnay, Scheurebe and Pinot Blanc. Alois Kracher made the area world-famous.
Why does Lake Neusiedl favour noble rot almost every year?
Autumn mists followed by sunny days
Mist then sun is the recipe for noble rot.

The town of Rust, on the west shore, has made Ausbruch since at least the 17th century, a sweet wine from botrytised berries mixed with base wine, similar to Tokaji Aszú. Its fame earned Rust the status of a free town in 1681. Ruster Ausbruch DAC protects it today; Furmint is being revived here for it.
Ruster Ausbruch is similar in method to Tokaji Aszú.
Yes. Botrytised berries are added to base wine.

Reading Burgenland and eating with it

Labels show the producer, grape, DAC, like Mittelburgenland DAC or Leithaberg DAC, and Reserve for riper wines. Sweet wines show the Prädikat, like TBA or Ausbruch. Austria's red, white and red stripe on the capsule, the Banderole, shows the wine has passed official testing.

Blaufränkisch suits roast duck, goose, venison and goulash, a Hungarian-Austrian dish with paprika. Zweigelt suits Wiener Schnitzel and grilled meat. Sweet wines from Neusiedlersee suit foie gras, blue cheese, strudel and fruit desserts. Serve Blaufränkisch at 16 to 18 degrees.
Paprika and rich meat suit its spice and acidity.
St. Martin's Day, November 11, is when Burgenland celebrates the new wine with roast goose. A perfect match for Blaufränkisch.
Which foods suit Neusiedlersee sweet wines?
